correctness.rationale: The bound itself is correct: independent modular computations give orders 6,20,21,110 modulo 9,25,49,121. Multiples preserve square divisibility, and a period of length 4620 contains 1034 classes from the first three orders and 1048 from all four, proving the lower bound 262/1155. The 14 extra classes are exactly 110k with gcd(k,6)=1 in that period. No density-existence assertion follows. The material defect is the characterization of Laniewski's result in the frozen Finding: the isolated abstract phrase 'on a set of exponents of density 47/210' is ambiguous, but the same v1 specifies lower density at least 47/210 in its introduction and precisely that liminf inequality in Corollary 6.20. The new bound rules out 47/210 as a possible exact density; it does not refute the preprint's stated density result.

originality.rationale: The decisive full text is Laniewski v1, Theorem 6.19 and Corollary 6.20. The general criterion there includes every multiple of 11·ord_11(2)=110. Using that theorem with one more small prime and counting its nonoverlapping residue classes is an immediate strengthening of the illustrative bound, not a distinct mechanism or a correction of the actual theorem. Coverage here means implication by the general theorem, not that 262/1155 was explicitly printed.
residual_risks: Other numerical lower bounds and earlier discussions were not exhaustively surveyed. The originality judgment uses affirmative general coverage from v1 and not any access failure. The abstract could still be made less ambiguous.

value.rationale: There would be value in refuting an exact-density theorem or deriving a substantive new lower-density mechanism. Here the source states a lower bound and already includes the extra progression in its all-primes criterion. The surviving arithmetic is a routine increment from one more small prime, with no sharpness or density-existence result; clarifying the abstract wording does not turn it into a new scientific finding.
